newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ c/a sustainable, confidence a trigger - Treasury.
newsitem.headline: NZ c/a sustainable, confidence a trigger - Treasury.

text.p: New Zealand's current acccount deficit is considered sustainable and driven by private sector investment, a paper released by Treasury shows.

"The composition of New Zealand's current account deficit suggests that it is presently sustainable," the paper, prepared for Treasurer Winston Peters and released to Reuters on Wednesday under the Official Information Act, said.

But it warned of the impact of a fall in business confidence and said if the deficit became a concern for international investors there could be a correction through a fall in the exchange rate and an increase in interest rates.
"For example, a correction could occur if consumer or businesss confidence was to decline due to lower firm profitability," it said.
Peters and Finance Minister Bill Birch have indicated their debut Budget, due on June 26, will see lower growth track and a lower budget surplus because of declining business confidence.

The paper was written as the Reserve Bank was finalising its economic projections, released on March 13, which forecast the current account deficit would be 5.8 percent of GDP in March 1997, up from 4.6 percent in the year to September 1996.
The RBNZ projected the deficit would rise to more than six percent of GDP over the next three years, or seven percent if migrant transfers were excluded.

"Current account deficits of this magnitude are unlikely to be sustained indefinitely," the RBNZ said in March, adding there was a risk in the three year forecast period of an adjustment through increased savings or substantial capital outflows.
In its December Economic and Fiscal Update the Treasury forecast the current account deficit would remain between 4.3 percent and 4.6 percent of GDP over the next three years.

"The current account deficit facing New Zealand is ultimately being driven by high levels of spending in New Zealand relative to national income and savings," the Treasury paper, prepared by macroeconomic policy manager David Grimmond, said.

"The national borrowing implied by the current account deficit is largely being used to fund private investment rather than consumption goods which is expected to increase the production potential of the economy."

"This reflects positively on the sustainablitity of economic growth and therefore the deficit. In addition strong growth in capital good imports is expected to have increased the production potential of the New Zealand economy," Grimmond said.
He said the decline in the current account in 1994 and 1995 was caused by a deteriorating balance of trade and balance on invisibles.
The current large deficit on invisibles was dictated by a large and sustained deficit on international investment flows.
"This is a result of the low level of investment by New Zealand firms overseas combined with high levels of foreign investment in New Zealand," Grimmond said.
Grimmond said a correction through capital outflows and higher interest rates would lead to reduced consumption and investment and consequently reduced inflationary pressures.
